currentContext.business: Kajaria manufactures and trades ceramic tiles, glazed vitrified tiles (GVT) and polished vitrified tiles (PVT) for residential, commercial and institutional applications, and extends the brand into complete bathroom solutions through Kerovit (sanitaryware and faucets) and into tile adhesives. It combines in-house production with strategic partnerships and outsourcing to preserve supply-chain flexibility, selling through a dealer and sub-dealer network to homeowners, architects, interior designers, developers and contractors as well as institutional customers such as builders, corporates and government agencies. The Company positions itself on premiumisation, brand-led demand and design differentiation across both new construction and the growing renovation segment.

currentContext.strengths: Distribution depth - a network of 1,800+ dealers that the Company says translates into rapid shelf availability for new categories such as adhesives, with cross-selling expanding wallet share|Brand-led, design-driven positioning supporting premiumisation and realisation-led growth, reinforced by engagement with architects, interior designers and institutional specifiers|Geographically diversified, automated manufacturing base that allows swift response to regional preferences, balancing scale with responsiveness|Supply-chain flexibility from combining in-house production with strategic partnerships - approximately 25% of supply remained strategically outsourced in FY26 to absorb demand fluctuations|Balance sheet strength: the Company describes negligible debt, a net cash position, strong cash flows and ample liquidity to fund growth in premiumisation, distribution and adjacent categories|Structural industry tailwinds it is positioned to capture - withdrawal of Chinese export subsidies, India's expanding network of Free Trade Agreements and gas-cost stress in the Morbi cluster are narrowing the branded-versus-unbranded price gap in favour of organised players
currentContext.strategies: Kajaria 2.0 - a company-wide reset built on four pillars: growing volumes and margins concurrently; replacing person-based decisions with system-based workflows; moving up the value chain into premium, higher-realisation categories; and rationalising SKUs, churning underperforming dealers, identifying white spaces and presenting one unified face to the market|Unify the three independent sales verticals - Ceramic, GVT and PVT - into a single structure so that dealers have one representative, one incentive policy and one Kajaria, delivering leaner operations and sharper accountability|Operation Manthan: a line-by-line diagnostic of every cost head, with non-essential hiring paused and Promoter Directors voluntarily forgoing salaries for the second successive year|Shift the manufacturing mix toward value leadership - convert the 9.1 MSM Gailpur line from ceramic floor tiles to Glazed Vitrified Tiles and commission a new 10 MSM line at Srikalahasti dedicated entirely to high-value products, with similar capacity under consideration at Gailpur|Build bathware (Kerovit) and adhesives from adjacencies into pillars - taking full ownership of the bathware CCPS holding and adding the newly commissioned Erode adhesives facility|Premiumisation and specifier-led selling: deepen engagement with architects, interior designers and institutional stakeholders to support realisation-led growth in aspirational segments|Deepen distribution in Tier 2 and Tier 3 towns to capture share as the branded-versus-unbranded price gap compresses|Institutionalise governance and control - vendor portal, automated vendor onboarding, real-time credential validation, automated workflows and stringent approval matrices made mandatory across all subsidiaries after the Kerovit Global incident|Sustainability as strategy - a biofuel mix at the northern plants that insulates the Company from natural gas prices while building a structural cost advantage, with ESG embedded in procurement, capital allocation and operating choices|Maintain a diversified, multi-fuel, multi-locational manufacturing footprint described as something no unorganised competitor can replicate, combining in-house production with strategic partnerships for supply-chain flexibility
currentContext.expansion: FY26 was framed as a shift from capacity-led growth to efficiency-led, value-driven manufacturing rather than a large greenfield tile build-out. The main tile action was purposeful upgrading of the existing base: a key unit at Gailpur was converted from ceramic floor tiles to Glazed Vitrified Tiles to align capacity with rising demand for premium formats, overlapping and slow-moving SKUs were cleaned up, and approximately 25% of supply remained strategically outsourced to give flexibility against demand fluctuations. In bathware, operations were streamlined by optimising newly installed kiln systems, adding advanced grinding and testing equipment and improving the dryer to cut fuel consumption, with the stated aim of improving operating leverage as scale increases and moving bathware toward sustained profitability. The clearest physical expansion is in tile adhesives: a dedicated 9,000 MT per month facility commenced operations in May 2025 at Gailpur, Rajasthan, and a second facility of similar capacity was planned at Erode, Tamil Nadu, to serve southern markets - the Erode plant, also 9,000 MT per month, started production in May 2026, with Kajaria Adhesive Private Limited converted into a wholly owned subsidiary during the year to establish that greenfield unit. On capital allocation, the Company describes a return-focused strategy prioritising maximum output from existing assets to absorb fixed costs and lift return on capital employed, with a balanced model of owned manufacturing and strategic outsourcing and 'cost-effective and technology-efficient capacity expansion'. Inorganically, the Board approved acquiring 44,11,764 CCPS of Kajaria Bathware Private Limited from Aravali Investment Holdings, Mauritius for Rs 50 Crore, taking the CCPS holding in KBPL to 100%. Separately, on April 30, 2026 the Board approved a share buyback that was subsequently completed. This bundle carries no rupee capex quantum: the named-disclosure blocks for capital commitments and segment capital expenditure arrived with labels only and no figures or units.
currentContext.mdna: Three structural shifts favour organised Indian manufacturers: China's progressive withdrawal of tile export subsidies opening previously closed markets; India's expanding network of Free Trade Agreements making exports more competitive; and unprecedented stress in the Morbi cluster from sharply rising gas prices|Industry volumes are expected to contract this year even as value grows, so as unbranded products retreat branded players are structurally positioned to capture a higher share of the market|Rising gas prices have forced widespread Morbi shutdowns and significant price hikes - a first for the cluster - compressing unbranded supply and narrowing the price gap versus branded manufacturers; as that gap compresses, consumer preference is expected to shift decisively towards branded products|Management describes the FY26 volume recovery as structural rather than cyclical: volumes began rising steadily from January 2026 with Q4 the strongest quarter, attributed to the unification strategy still early in its value creation|Trend cited after the financial year: the first quarter, with the exception of April 2026, also registered double-digit volume growth (the sentence is cut short in this bundle)|Margin levers named: regained pricing power, pricing actions following the LNG supply disruption, improved product mix towards premium vitrified and large-format tiles, Operation Manthan cost optimisation and packaging/procurement efficiencies|Outlook per the Directors' Report: India's tile industry is entering a period of structural recovery supported by sustained economic expansion, rising disposable incomes and accelerating real estate development in Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities|Enhanced capacity utilisation is expected to unlock operating leverage, and disciplined working capital management to further strengthen liquidity|Macro backdrop cited: India among the fastest-growing major economies in FY26 with provisional real GDP growth around 7.7%, offset by external volatility, uneven export demand and inflationary pressures that created a more measured operating environment|Risk to the demand narrative flagged by analysts and acknowledged by management: that a significant portion of the volume uplift came from supply disruptions caused by the ongoing conflict in the Middle East rather than underlying demand strength|Branded penetration in tile adhesives remains well below mature-market benchmarks, leaving a long runway for growth, aided by the shift from unorganised cement-sand mortar to branded installation systems|Bathware demand execution: dealer-network expansion, 20 new sanitaryware products and new faucet concepts, plus a strengthened leadership bench (a Chief Business Officer and a senior advisor recruited from a leading bathware company)

risks.risk: Sustainability of the FY26 volume recovery - the uplift may be a supply-disruption windfall rather than real demand
risks.note: The MD&A itself records the critical question raised by analysts and investors: that a significant portion of the volume uplift is attributable to supply disruptions caused by the ongoing conflict in the Middle East rather than to underlying demand strength. Management counters that the recovery is structural, citing volumes rising steadily from January 2026 and Q4 as the strongest quarter, but the burden of proof sits with FY27 delivery.

risks.risk: Energy cost and gas supply exposure
risks.note: Q4 margin expansion is explicitly attributed to pricing actions following the LNG supply disruption, and the wider tile industry backdrop is one of sharply rising gas prices. Fuel is a primary input for tile and sanitaryware firing, so gas price and availability swings feed straight into cost of production and into the pricing environment the Company can sustain.

The MD&A reports tiles at 88.6% of FY26 topline, against 8.6% for bathware and 2.8% for tile adhesives, with the traded plywood business discontinued during the year. The diversification verticals are still small, so a downturn in tile demand or realisation cannot be offset elsewhere; the MD&A also notes industry volumes are expected to contract this year even as value grows.

risks.risk: Execution and channel risk from the Kajaria 2.0 restructuring
risks.note: Muted volume growth through the first nine months of FY26 is attributed to intensive reconstruction while laying the foundations of Kajaria 2.0 - the unification of three tile verticals, SKU rationalisation and capacity optimisation. Management itself describes the unification strategy as still in its early stages of value creation, so the payback remains unproven and further disruption during roll-out is possible.

risks.risk: Input cost volatility and demand moderation
risks.note: Management describes a challenging industry environment marked by input cost volatility and selective demand moderation, with cost pressures cited alongside muted volumes in the first nine months. Margin recovery in FY26 rested on regained pricing power and cost optimisation, both of which are reversible if input costs run ahead of realisation again.

risks.risk: Competitive pressure from the unorganised segment and the Morbi cluster
risks.note: The Company's thesis depends on the branded-versus-informal price gap continuing to compress as Morbi faces gas-driven shutdowns and price hikes. If gas costs normalise and unbranded supply returns, the price differential could widen again and the expected shift in consumer preference towards branded products would slow.

risks.risk: Regulatory change from the New Labour Codes
risks.note: The MD&A flags that the New Labour Codes on Wages, Social Security, Industrial Relations and Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions will bring significant structural changes to workforce management across India's manufacturing sector. Kajaria has assessed compensation structures, leave entitlements, social security obligations and contract labour arrangements and is recalibrating payroll and HR processes, but the cost impact lands on a workforce that is heavily contract-based - 2,920 of 4,995 workers are other than permanent.

BRSR reports permanent employee turnover of 19% and permanent worker turnover of 18% in FY 2025-26, both marginally higher than the prior year, in a business where the leadership team's deep sectoral experience is named as a core mitigant. Women are 4% of employees, 3% of workers, 1 of 9 Board of Directors members (11.11%) and none of the 2 Key Management Personnel, and no differently abled employees or workers are reported.

risks.risk: Internal control and process dependency risk
risks.note: The Board states confidence in internal control adequacy, but the FY26 remediation itself points to the exposure: under Operation Manthan the Company automated vendor onboarding, replacing manual workflows with a system-driven framework that standardises documentation. Until such controls are fully embedded, process integrity depends on the ERP and business process MIS monitoring plus regular Internal Auditor and Cost Auditor review reported to the Audit Committee and the Board.

Exports are just 0.51% of total turnover against 12 national plants, 46 national offices and 36 states/UTs served, so earnings are almost wholly geared to Indian construction and renovation demand. The MD&A's own opportunity case - the phased withdrawal of Chinese export subsidies and India's expanding network of Free Trade Agreements opening new export corridors - is therefore an option the Company has barely exercised.

one-line thesis: Kajaria leveraged the Morbi cluster shutdown (due to gas shortages) and prior sales unification efforts to drive 11% volume growth and expand EBITDA margins to 19.2% via price hikes, positioning itself to capture significant market share as unorganized competitors face structural cost disadvantages. While Q1 faces transient production lags from the Morbi restart, the medium-term outlook favors consolidated players with multi-location assets and biofuel flexibility.
financial scorecard: Revenue: INR 1,373 cr (+12% YoY); EBITDA: INR 263 cr (Margin 19.19% vs 10.01% YoY); PAT: INR 136 cr (+216% YoY) driven by volume mix and realization; Order Book: Not disclosed (Make-to-Stock model); Net Debt: Net Cash position (implied by buyback rationale and working capital improvement); One-offs: Morbi plant shutdown in March reduced production by 7% despite sales growth; Accounting note: Presentation error corrected swapping inventory/debtors figures.
guidance: Revenue Growth: No specific guidance given (management cites external volatility); Margin: Targeting 18-19% range; Order Inflow: Momentum positive post-Jan '26, Q1 seasonally weak but YoY April expected strong; Capex/Commissioning: Morbi plants restarted April 16; full capacity running.
order book & pipeline: N/A (Inventory-driven model); Finished Goods Inventory reduced by ~1.5 million sqm in March to ~11 million sqm total; Days Sales Inventory improved significantly contributing to 14-day reduction in working capital cycle (51 days).
segment / subsidiary detail: Tiles: INR 1,212 cr (+11% YoY); Bathware: INR 117 cr (+6% YoY); Adhesives: INR 44 cr (+110% YoY). Tiles remain core driver; Adhesives showing high base growth.
growth verticals / optionality: Market share gain from Morbi unorganized cluster (estimated 150-160 plants running vs 500+ previously); Adhesive segment scaling; Potential for further pricing power as cost differential widens for competitors.
margins & cost dynamics: EBITDA margin expanded to 19.19% (vs 10.01% YoY) due to 12-17% price hikes covering gas inflation; Fuel cost mix: North ~INR 62.5/scm (April), South/West ~INR 79-81/scm; Biofuel usage ~15-30% in North spray dryers providing cost arbitrage vs pure gas players.
capex / expansion: No major greenfield capex announced; Focus on restarting Morbi JV/outsourced capacity; Maintenance capex ongoing.
capital allocation: Buyback approved to return surplus cash (tax-efficient vs dividends) and improve ROE; Working capital optimization priority (cycle down to 51 days).
risks & watch-items: Sustained high gas prices impacting demand elasticity; Propane ban permanence for industry; Morbi competitors restarting faster than expected; Geopolitical impact on freight costs (UAE freight up to $4k) hurting export potential.
management quality / tone: Confident and opportunistic regarding competitor distress; Cautious on providing specific numerical guidance due to macro volatility; Emphasizes structural advantage of multi-location footprint.
non-obvious takeaways: Management highlighted that Morbi competitors face a 35-40% cost hike (vs Kajaria's 15-16% price increase) due to lower base prices and higher gas dependency, creating a permanent margin gap; Export market effectively closed for Morbi due to freight spikes ($300 to $4000 to UAE), forcing all supply into domestic market but at uncompetitive prices.

| High exposure to Morbi cluster disruptions and lack of biofuel/alternative fuel infrastructure compared to organized peers. | Unlisted Morbi Manufacturers | loser | High | Facing existential cost crisis; many plants remain shut or operating at low utilization; forced to raise prices 35-40% which demand may not bear. |

themes.title: Building-materials & home-improvement up-cycle
themes.need: The residential up-cycle pulls a broad finishing/home-improvement basket - tiles & sanitaryware (KAJARIACER/CERA/SOMANYCERA/ORIENTBELL/HINDWAREAP), wood-panels & laminates (CENTURYPLY/GREENPANEL/GREENLAM/RUSHIL/STYLAMIND), pipes/adhesives (PIDILITIND/SUPREMEIND/ASTRAL-tier) and paints (ASIANPAINT/CARYSIL/SIRCA). Premiumization + GST formalization shift share to organized players.
themes.driver: Festive/real-estate completion demand; GST 2.0 + commodity tailwinds; capacity commissioning and channel restocking.

one_liner.title: One Liner (RHP)
one_liner.body: Kajaria Ceramics is one of India's most integrated, consumer-facing building materials companies, anchored by a ceramic and vitrified tile business that contributed about 88.6% of FY26 topline, with adjacent bathware and tile-adhesive verticals.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: Kajaria manufactures and trades ceramic tiles, glazed vitrified tiles (GVT) and polished vitrified tiles (PVT) for residential, commercial and institutional applications, and extends the brand into complete bathroom solutions through Kerovit (sanitaryware and faucets) and into tile adhesives. It combines in-house production with strategic partnerships and outsourcing to preserve supply-chain flexibility, selling through a dealer and sub-dealer network to homeowners, architects, interior designers, developers and contractors as well as institutional customers such as builders, corporates and government agencies. The Company positions itself on premiumisation, brand-led demand and design differentiation across both new construction and the growing renovation segment.

guidance.title: Guidance
guidance.body: Revenue Growth: No specific guidance given (management cites external volatility); Margin: Targeting 18-19% range; Order Inflow: Momentum positive post-Jan '26, Q1 seasonally weak but YoY April expected strong; Capex/Commissioning: Morbi plants restarted April 16; full capacity running.

growth_optionality.title: Growth verticals / optionality
growth_optionality.body: Market share gain from Morbi unorganized cluster (estimated 150-160 plants running vs 500+ previously); Adhesive segment scaling; Potential for further pricing power as cost differential widens for competitors.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Three structural shifts favour organised Indian manufacturers: China's progressive withdrawal of tile export subsidies opening previously closed markets; India's expanding network of Free Trade Agreements making exports more competitive; and unprecedented stress in the Morbi cluster from sharply rising gas prices
- Industry volumes are expected to contract this year even as value grows, so as unbranded products retreat branded players are structurally positioned to capture a higher share of the market
- Rising gas prices have forced widespread Morbi shutdowns and significant price hikes - a first for the cluster - compressing unbranded supply and narrowing the price gap versus branded manufacturers; as that gap compresses, consumer preference is expected to shift decisively towards branded products
- Management describes the FY26 volume recovery as structural rather than cyclical: volumes began rising steadily from January 2026 with Q4 the strongest quarter, attributed to the unification strategy still early in its value creation
- Trend cited after the financial year: the first quarter, with the exception of April 2026, also registered double-digit volume growth (the sentence is cut short in this bundle)
- Margin levers named: regained pricing power, pricing actions following the LNG supply disruption, improved product mix towards premium vitrified and large-format tiles, Operation Manthan cost optimisation and packaging/procurement efficiencies
- Outlook per the Directors' Report: India's tile industry is entering a period of structural recovery supported by sustained economic expansion, rising disposable incomes and accelerating real estate development in Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities
- Enhanced capacity utilisation is expected to unlock operating leverage, and disciplined working capital management to further strengthen liquidity
- Macro backdrop cited: India among the fastest-growing major economies in FY26 with provisional real GDP growth around 7.7%, offset by external volatility, uneven export demand and inflationary pressures that created a more measured operating environment
- Risk to the demand narrative flagged by analysts and acknowledged by management: that a significant portion of the volume uplift came from supply disruptions caused by the ongoing conflict in the Middle East rather than underlying demand strength
- Branded penetration in tile adhesives remains well below mature-market benchmarks, leaving a long runway for growth, aided by the shift from unorganised cement-sand mortar to branded installation systems
- Bathware demand execution: dealer-network expansion, 20 new sanitaryware products and new faucet concepts, plus a strengthened leadership bench (a Chief Business Officer and a senior advisor recruited from a leading bathware company)

margins.title: Margins & cost dynamics
margins.body: EBITDA margin expanded to 19.19% (vs 10.01% YoY) due to 12-17% price hikes covering gas inflation; Fuel cost mix: North ~INR 62.5/scm (April), South/West ~INR 79-81/scm; Biofuel usage ~15-30% in North spray dryers providing cost arbitrage vs pure gas players.

capital_allocation.title: Capital allocation
capital_allocation.body: Buyback approved to return surplus cash (tax-efficient vs dividends) and improve ROE; Working capital optimization priority (cycle down to 51 days).

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: FY26 was framed as a shift from capacity-led growth to efficiency-led, value-driven manufacturing rather than a large greenfield tile build-out. The main tile action was purposeful upgrading of the existing base: a key unit at Gailpur was converted from ceramic floor tiles to Glazed Vitrified Tiles to align capacity with rising demand for premium formats, overlapping and slow-moving SKUs were cleaned up, and approximately 25% of supply remained strategically outsourced to give flexibility against demand fluctuations. In bathware, operations were streamlined by optimising newly installed kiln systems, adding advanced grinding and testing equipment and improving the dryer to cut fuel consumption, with the stated aim of improving operating leverage as scale increases and moving bathware toward sustained profitability. The clearest physical expansion is in tile adhesives: a dedicated 9,000 MT per month facility commenced operations in May 2025 at Gailpur, Rajasthan, and a second facility of similar capacity was planned at Erode, Tamil Nadu, to serve southern markets - the Erode plant, also 9,000 MT per month, started production in May 2026, with Kajaria Adhesive Private Limited converted into a wholly owned subsidiary during the year to establish that greenfield unit. On capital allocation, the Company describes a return-focused strategy prioritising maximum output from existing assets to absorb fixed costs and lift return on capital employed, with a balanced model of owned manufacturing and strategic outsourcing and 'cost-effective and technology-efficient capacity expansion'. Inorganically, the Board approved acquiring 44,11,764 CCPS of Kajaria Bathware Private Limited from Aravali Investment Holdings, Mauritius for Rs 50 Crore, taking the CCPS holding in KBPL to 100%. Separately, on April 30, 2026 the Board approved a share buyback that was subsequently completed. This bundle carries no rupee capex quantum: the named-disclosure blocks for capital commitments and segment capital expenditure arrived with labels only and no figures or units.

management_tone.title: Management quality / tone
management_tone.body: Confident and opportunistic regarding competitor distress; Cautious on providing specific numerical guidance due to macro volatility; Emphasizes structural advantage of multi-location footprint.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Distribution depth - a network of 1,800+ dealers that the Company says translates into rapid shelf availability for new categories such as adhesives, with cross-selling expanding wallet share
- Brand-led, design-driven positioning supporting premiumisation and realisation-led growth, reinforced by engagement with architects, interior designers and institutional specifiers
- Geographically diversified, automated manufacturing base that allows swift response to regional preferences, balancing scale with responsiveness
- Supply-chain flexibility from combining in-house production with strategic partnerships - approximately 25% of supply remained strategically outsourced in FY26 to absorb demand fluctuations
- Balance sheet strength: the Company describes negligible debt, a net cash position, strong cash flows and ample liquidity to fund growth in premiumisation, distribution and adjacent categories
- Structural industry tailwinds it is positioned to capture - withdrawal of Chinese export subsidies, India's expanding network of Free Trade Agreements and gas-cost stress in the Morbi cluster are narrowing the branded-versus-unbranded price gap in favour of organised players

risks.title: Risks & watch-items
risks.body: Sustained high gas prices impacting demand elasticity; Propane ban permanence for industry; Morbi competitors restarting faster than expected; Geopolitical impact on freight costs (UAE freight up to $4k) hurting export potential.

non_obvious.title: Non-obvious takeaways
non_obvious.body: Management highlighted that Morbi competitors face a 35-40% cost hike (vs Kajaria's 15-16% price increase) due to lower base prices and higher gas dependency, creating a permanent margin gap; Export market effectively closed for Morbi due to freight spikes ($300 to $4000 to UAE), forcing all supply into domestic market but at uncompetitive prices.

strategy.title: Strategies (RHP)
strategy.body:
- Kajaria 2.0 - a company-wide reset built on four pillars: growing volumes and margins concurrently; replacing person-based decisions with system-based workflows; moving up the value chain into premium, higher-realisation categories; and rationalising SKUs, churning underperforming dealers, identifying white spaces and presenting one unified face to the market
- Unify the three independent sales verticals - Ceramic, GVT and PVT - into a single structure so that dealers have one representative, one incentive policy and one Kajaria, delivering leaner operations and sharper accountability
- Operation …
